lead: An avalanche photodiode (APD) gives the photodiode internal current gain. One photon still creates one primary electron–hole pair, but a high-field region near breakdown makes each carrier knock out more pairs by impact ionisation, so the current leaves multiplied by a gain M. The multiplication is random and adds excess noise, so there is a best gain rather than "the more the better". APDs are used where the received light is weak and the amplifier noise would otherwise swamp the signal: long links without optical amplifiers, and optical time-domain reflectometers.
prereq: You need responsivity from Detection principles and the PIN structure from PN and PIN photodiodes.

blocks.text: A photon absorbed in the depleted absorption layer creates one primary electron–hole pair, exactly as in a PIN. In a PIN that pair gives one electron of external current. In an APD the carrier then drifts into a thin gain region where the field is close to the breakdown field (more than about 10⁵ V/cm). Between collisions it gains enough energy to knock a bound electron into the conduction band, creating a new electron–hole pair. This is impact ionisation.

The new carriers are accelerated too and can ionise again, so one primary pair sets off a cascade. A common structure, the reach-through APD, is a stack n⁺–p–π–p⁺: light is absorbed in the wide, lightly doped π layer, and electrons drift into the thin p layer next to the n⁺ contact, where the field is highest and the gain happens.

blocks.where: M is the avalanche gain (multiplication factor); I<sub>M</sub> is the multiplied output current and I<sub>p</sub> = RP is the primary photocurrent the same light would give with no gain. Typical APDs run at M = 10 to 100.

This is an empirical fit. V is the reverse bias, V<sub>B</sub> the breakdown voltage and n a fitting number, about 3 to 6. Far below V<sub>B</sub>, M stays near 1; close to V<sub>B</sub> it rises very steeply. With V<sub>B</sub> = 50 V and n = 3, M = 10 needs V = 50 × 0.9<sup>1/3</sup> = 48.3 V.

sections.h3: Excess noise and the best gain

blocks.text: Multiplication is random: two primary carriers seldom produce the same number of secondary pairs. So the multiplied current fluctuates more than plain shot noise of the same current. This extra spread is the excess noise factor F(M) ≥ 1. It depends on k, the ratio of the hole ionisation rate to the electron ionisation rate (for electrons starting the avalanche).

blocks.where: F is the excess noise factor, M the gain and k the ionisation-rate ratio. If only electrons ionise, k = 0 and F = 2 − 1/M, never more than 2. If both carriers ionise equally, k = 1 and F = M, the worst case. Silicon has k ≈ 0.02 to 0.05; InGaAs APDs with InP gain regions have k ≈ 0.5; germanium is near 1. A rough fit sometimes used is F ≈ M<sup>x</sup>, with x ≈ 0.3 for Si and 0.7 for InGaAs.
ish² is the mean-square shot-noise current at the APD output in A², q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and B is the receiver bandwidth in Hz. Dark current adds its own term; see Photodetector noise.

blocks.text: The receiver also has thermal noise i<sub>th</sub>² from its load or amplifier, which does not depend on M. The signal power is (MI<sub>p</sub>)². At small M the thermal noise dominates, and SNR grows almost as M². At large M the multiplied shot noise dominates: signal and noise both carry M², but F keeps growing with M, so SNR falls. In between is an optimum M<sub>opt</sub>. For a thermal-noise-limited receiver a good estimate is M<sub>opt</sub> ≈ [4k<sub>B</sub>T/(kqR<sub>L</sub>I<sub>p</sub>)]<sup>1/3</sup>, with k<sub>B</sub> = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K Boltzmann's constant. A smaller k gives a larger M<sub>opt</sub>.

Silicon APDs have low k and low excess noise, and they work well at 0.8–0.9 µm. At 1.3–1.55 µm the absorber must be InGaAs, but avalanche gain inside InGaAs is noisy and leaks at the high fields needed. The separate absorption and multiplication (SAM) APD solves this: an InGaAs layer absorbs the light at a moderate field, and an InP layer next to it does the multiplication at high field.

An APD needs a much higher bias than a PIN: tens of volts for InGaAs/InP and up to a few hundred volts for some silicon reach-through APDs, always just below breakdown. Breakdown voltage rises with temperature, so at a fixed bias M falls as the diode warms. An APD receiver therefore has a temperature-compensated bias supply or a gain-control loop. The avalanche also takes time to build up, and the gain–bandwidth product is roughly fixed: higher M means lower bandwidth.

examples.question: An InGaAs/InP APD has η = 0.8 at λ = 1.3 µm, gain M = 10 and ionisation ratio k = 0.3. It receives P = 100 nW, and the receiver bandwidth is B = 1 GHz. The amplifier's thermal noise is that of R<sub>L</sub> = 1 kΩ at T = 300 K. Find the multiplied current, F, the shot and thermal noise, and the SNR. Compare with a PIN (M = 1) of the same η.
steps: Primary photocurrent: I<sub>p</sub> = RP = 0.839 × 100 × 10⁻⁹ = 83.9 nA. Multiplied current: I<sub>M</sub> = MI<sub>p</sub> = 839 nA.

SNR = I<sub>M</sub>²/(i<sub>sh</sub>² + i<sub>th</sub>²) = (839 × 10⁻⁹)²/(2.82 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 7.04 × 10⁻¹³/2.82 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 25.0, or 10 log₁₀ 25.0 = 14.0 dB. (Shot noise alone would give 60.5, or 17.8 dB; leaving out the thermal noise overstates the SNR.)

PIN, M = 1: signal (83.9 nA)² = 7.04 × 10⁻¹⁵ A²; shot 2qI<sub>p</sub>B = 2.69 × 10⁻¹⁷ A²; thermal 1.66 × 10⁻¹⁴ A². SNR = 7.04 × 10⁻¹⁵/1.66 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 0.424, or −3.7 dB. The APD gains 14.0 − (−3.7) = 17.7 dB.

Is M = 10 the best? M<sub>opt</sub> ≈ [4k<sub>B</sub>T/(kqR<sub>L</sub>I<sub>p</sub>)]<sup>1/3</sup> = [1.656 × 10⁻²⁰/(0.3 × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1000 × 83.9 × 10⁻⁹)]<sup>1/3</sup> = 4108<sup>1/3</sup> = 16. At M = 16, F = 6.16 and SNR = 14.9 dB, only 0.9 dB better than at M = 10.
examples.answer: I<sub>M</sub> = 0.839 µA, F = 4.33, shot noise 108 nA rms, thermal noise 129 nA rms, SNR = 25.0 (14.0 dB) against −3.7 dB for the PIN. The best gain is about 16, giving 14.9 dB.

traps: Multiplying only the signal and forgetting the excess noise. Signal power grows as M², shot-noise power as M²F.
Saying a bigger M always helps. Past M<sub>opt</sub> the extra excess noise outweighs the extra gain, and SNR falls (in the example, 14.7 dB at M = 20 against 14.9 dB at M = 16).
Confusing the ionisation ratio k with the gain M, or with Boltzmann's constant k<sub>B</sub>.
Writing the SNR from shot noise only. At moderate gain the amplifier's thermal noise is often the larger term.
Using F = M for every APD. That is the worst case, k = 1; a silicon APD with k = 0.02 at M = 100 has F = 0.02 × 100 + 0.98 × 1.99 = 3.95.

quiz.q: Define the avalanche gain M and give its typical range.
quiz.a: M = I<sub>M</sub>/I<sub>p</sub>, the multiplied output current over the primary photocurrent. Typical APDs run at M = 10 to 100.

quiz.q: Why does the excess noise factor depend on k, and which value of k is better?
quiz.a: k is the hole-to-electron ionisation-rate ratio. When both carriers ionise, carriers travel back and forth and the chain is more random, so F is larger. Small k is better; k = 0 gives F = 2 − 1/M.

quiz.q: An APD has M = 20 and k = 0.2. Calculate F.
An APD with V<sub>B</sub> = 50 V and n = 3 is biased at 48 V. Find M from the empirical formula.
Explain why an APD has an optimum gain.
quiz.a: At low M the M-independent thermal noise dominates, so SNR grows about as M². At high M the multiplied shot noise 2qI<sub>p</sub>M²FB dominates; signal and noise both grow as M² but F also grows, so SNR falls. The maximum lies in between; for the worked example it is at M ≈ 16.

quiz.q: Why is a separate absorption and multiplication (SAM) structure used for 1.3–1.55 µm APDs?
quiz.a: InGaAs absorbs well at these wavelengths but multiplies noisily and leaks at high field. SAM uses InGaAs only to absorb and InP to multiply.

quiz.q: The bias of an APD is raised so that M doubles while F stays the same. What happens to the signal power and the shot-noise power?
quiz.a: Signal current doubles, so signal power is four times larger. Shot-noise power contains M², so it is also four times larger.

quiz.q: Why does an APD receiver need temperature compensation of its bias?
quiz.a: Breakdown voltage rises with temperature. At a fixed bias, V/V<sub>B</sub> then changes, so M drifts away from its optimum (down when warm, up towards breakdown when cold).

beyond: Not for the exam. Low-noise APDs use InAlAs gain layers (lower k than InP) and, in research, antimony-based alloys and mercury cadmium telluride, which can have k close to zero. Single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) are biased above breakdown so that one photon triggers a full avalanche; they are used in lidar and quantum key distribution. Search next for "InAlAs APD", "excess noise factor measurement" and "SPAD".

figure.caption: Top: a reach-through APD. Light is absorbed in the wide π layer, and electrons drift into the thin high-field p layer, where impact ionisation multiplies them. Bottom: SNR of the worked example against gain. It rises from −3.7 dB at M = 1 to 14.0 dB at M = 10 and peaks near M = 16, after which excess noise wins.

spec.aria: Top: layers n plus, p gain region, wide pi absorption region, p plus, with the field highest in the p layer. Bottom: SNR in decibels against gain M on a log scale from 1 to 200, rising from minus 3.7 dB at M equals 1 to 14.0 dB at M equals 10, peaking at 14.9 dB near M equals 16 and falling at higher gain.
